title: a young woman says yes
tomorrow: the words, line by line, from Luke

cards: A small town in Galilee called Nazareth. A young woman there is promised in marriage to a man named Joseph. Luke doesn't give her age, and he doesn't describe the house.

An ordinary day, as far as we know. And then, Luke's Gospel says, the angel Gabriel comes in to her, telling her she's going to have a child, and that he'll be called the Son of the Most High. She isn't married yet.
Today, a yes the whole Catholic story leans on, and the young woman who said it.

teach.b: Her name, in Hebrew, was Miriam, like the sister of Moses. We say Mary.
And the first thing Gabriel says to her, after the greeting, is what the angels in Luke say again and again: "Fear not, Mary, for thou hast found grace with God." Grace: yesterday's word, back again.
Then she does something people skip over.
She asks a question. How can this be? She isn't passive.

She wants to understand. The angel answers, and then she gives the reply Catholics have treasured ever since. In the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word."
In Latin, be it done is fiat, and Catholics still call her answer Mary's fiat. Her yes. Here's why it matters so much.
Catholics say God didn't force anything on her. He asked, and waited, and the whole story of Jesus turns on a young woman saying yes.
That's why they call her the Mother of God, because they believe her son is God, and why she gets the highest honor of any saint: honor, as day five said, not worship.

teach.h: BEHOLD THE HANDMAID OF THE LORD.
teach.b: Other Christians differ on how much to say about her. Many Protestants honor her as a faithful believer and a model of trust, and don't pray to her.
And Luke's page is the same for all of them: a young woman, a question, and then yes.

how: Catholics honor Mary as the Mother of God and ask for her prayers, especially in the Hail Mary and the rosary; the Annunciation, the angel's visit, has its own feast day each year.

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.

s: Catholics honor Mary and ask for her prayers; worship, in Catholic teaching, belongs to God alone.
Mary asks the angel a question before she agrees
she asks how this can be. then she says yes.
the Gospels tell us Mary's exact age
they don't. Luke calls her a virgin promised in marriage and says nothing about her age.

games.q: you're a young woman in Nazareth. an angel tells you you'll have a child before you're married. what does Mary do first?
games.why: she asks a real question, hears the answer, and then says: be it done to me according to thy word.

practice: Here's the practice. Think of one thing in your life right now that you're resisting: something you can't change and keep pushing against. Name it.
Notice how tightly you're holding it. Then, breath by breath, let your hands open a little on your lap. If you pray, you can borrow Mary's words: be it done to me.

wordCard.voice: Mary. Miriam of Nazareth, the mother of Jesus, whose yes, her fiat, Catholics honor above every other saint. Ninth word.

orig.note: Latin: let it be done. from Luke 1:38 in the Latin Bible, fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum.

carryVoice: Your line: let it be. But notice the order: first she asked her honest question. Day nine.
